Mesillat Yesharim 21:7: However, what can protect a person and save him from these undermining factors is trust — namely, that he should cast his burden entirely upon the Lord, knowing with certainty that it is impossible for a person to lack what has been allotted to him, as our Sages, of blessed memory, said in their statements (Beitzah 16a): a person's entire sustenance is allotted to him from Rosh Hashanah, etc. And so they said (Yoma 38b): no person touches what is prepared for his fellow even by a hairsbreadth.
Mesillat Yesharim 21:8: And a person could indeed sit idle and the decree would still be fulfilled, were it not that a penalty was imposed beforehand on all mankind (Genesis 3:19): "by the sweat of your brow shall you eat bread" — therefore a person is obligated to make some effort for the sake of his livelihood, for so the Supernal King has decreed.
Mesillat Yesharim 21:9: And this is like a tax that the entire human race must pay, from which there is no escape. Therefore they said (Sifrei): one might think, even if he sits idle he will receive his sustenance — therefore Scripture says: "in all the work of your hands that you do" (Deuteronomy 28:12).
Mesillat Yesharim 21:10: But it is not the effort itself that is effective; rather, the effort is required, and once he has made the effort, he has discharged his obligation, and there is already room for the blessing of Heaven to rest upon him, and he need not spend his days in diligence and striving. This is what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 75:7-8): "For not from the east, nor from the west... for God is the judge, etc." And King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 23:4): "Do not weary yourself to become rich; cease from your own understanding."
Mesillat Yesharim 21:11: Rather, the true way is the way of the early pious ones, who made their Torah study primary and their work secondary, and both were sustained in their hands; for once a person has done a small amount of work, from then on he need only trust in his Maker and not grieve over any worldly matter — then his mind will remain free and his heart ready for true piety and perfect service.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:1:
An Explanation of the Trait of Humility and Its Components
Now, we have already spoken above of the disgrace of pride, and from this the praise of humility can be inferred; but now let us explain, more as a fundamental matter, humility itself, and pride will become clear of itself.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:2: Behold, the general principle of humility is that a person should not esteem himself for any reason whatsoever — this is precisely the opposite of pride, and the consequences that follow from it will be the opposite of the consequences of pride.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:3: And when we examine it closely, we find that it depends on both thought and deed, for first a person must be humble in his thought, and afterward conduct himself in the ways of the humble.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:4: For if he is not humble in his mind, and yet wishes to be humble in deed, he will be nothing but one of the false and evil humble ones we mentioned above, who belong to the category of hypocrites, than whom there is no worse evil in the world. Let us now explain these components.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:5: Humility in thought is that a person should reflect and become convinced that praise and honor are not fitting for him — all the more so raising himself above the rest of his kind — both because of what he necessarily lacks, and because of what he already possesses.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:6: Because of what he lacks: it is obvious that it is impossible for any person, at whatever level of perfection he may be, not to have many deficiencies — whether from the side of his own nature, or from the side of his family and relatives, or from the side of incidents that have befallen him, or from the side of his own deeds, for "there is not a righteous man upon earth who does good and does not sin" (Ecclesiastes 7:20). Behold, all these are blemishes in a person that leave him no room for self-exaltation at all, even if he possesses many virtues, for these very deficiencies are already enough to darken them.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:7: Behold, wisdom is what brings a person more than anything else to self-exaltation and pride, since it is already a virtue that belongs to the person himself, in his most honored part, namely, his intellect.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:8: And behold, there is no wise man who does not err, and who does not need to learn from the words of his fellows, and many times even from the words of his own students. If so, then, how could he exalt himself over his wisdom?
Mesillat Yesharim 22:9: And indeed, whoever possesses upright understanding, even if he has merited to be a truly great and outstanding sage, when he looks and reflects, will see that there is no room for pride and self-exaltation. For whoever possesses an intellect such that he knows more than others does nothing but what is the law of his nature to do — like a bird that soars in flight because it is its nature, or an ox that pulls with its strength because that is its rule. So too, whoever is wise is so because his nature brings him to it; and if the one who is not now as wise as he had a natural intellect like his, he too would have grown wise as he did. If so, then, there is no place here for self-exaltation and pride,
Mesillat Yesharim 22:10: but rather, if he possesses great wisdom, he is obligated to teach it to whoever needs it, as Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai said (Avot 2:9): if you have learned much Torah, do not take credit for yourself, for it is for this that you were created.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:11: If he is rich, let him rejoice in his portion, and it is upon him to help whoever lacks; if he is mighty, let him help the failing and rescue the oppressed.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:12: To what may this be compared? To the servants of a household, each of whom is appointed over some particular task, and it is fitting for him to stand at his post according to his assignment, to complete the work of the household and its needs — and there is truly no room for pride here.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:13: And this is the reflection and contemplation fitting for every person whose intellect is upright and not stubborn; and once this becomes clear to him, he will be called truly humble, humble in his heart and within himself. This is like the matter of David, who said to Michal (II Samuel 6:22): "and I will be lowly in my own eyes."
Mesillat Yesharim 22:14: And they said, of blessed memory (Sotah 5b): How great are the lowly of spirit! For at the time when the Temple stood, if a person brought a burnt-offering, he received the reward of a burnt-offering; if a meal-offering, he received the reward of a meal-offering; but whoever possesses a lowly spirit — Scripture accounts it to him as though he had offered all the offerings, as it is said (Psalms 51:19): "The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit,"
Mesillat Yesharim 22:15: this being the praise of the lowly of spirit, who are humble in their hearts and their thoughts.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:16: And they further said (Chullin 89a): "not because you were more numerous than any other people" (Deuteronomy 7:7) — the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them: My children, I desire you because even when I bestow greatness upon you, you make yourselves small before Me. I gave greatness to Abraham, and he said, "and I am dust and ashes" (Genesis 18:27); I gave greatness to Moses and Aaron, and they said, "and what are we?" (Exodus 16:7); I gave greatness to David, and he said, "and I am a worm, and no man" (Psalms 22:7).
Mesillat Yesharim 22:17: All this is because the upright heart does not let itself be enticed by any virtue that comes into its possession, knowing truly that it is not thereby freed from its lowliness, because of the other deficiencies that must inevitably remain in it; and further, that even in those very virtues he has attained, he certainly has not reached the final degree.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:18: And further, even if there were no other deficiency in him, his simply being flesh and blood, born of woman, is enough and more than enough for lowliness and inferiority, so that self-exaltation is not fitting for him at all; for every virtue that he attains is nothing but the kindness of God upon him, who wishes to be gracious to him even though, by his own nature and materiality, he is exceedingly lowly and despicable — therefore he has no choice but to give thanks to the One who has been gracious to him, and to be ever more submissive.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:19: To what may this be compared? To a poor and destitute man who receives a gift out of kindness, who cannot help but be ashamed; for the more the kindness he receives increases, the more his shame increases. So it is with every person whose eyes are open to see himself, when he attains good virtues from the Name, blessed be He — in the vein of what King David said (Psalms 116:12): "What shall I render to the Lord for all His bounties toward me?"
Mesillat Yesharim 22:20: And we have already seen great pious men who were punished for taking credit for themselves, despite all their piety:
Mesillat Yesharim 22:21: Nechemiah ben Chachalyah — they said, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 93b): Why was his book not called by his own name? Because he took credit for himself.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:22: And likewise Hezekiah said (Isaiah 38:17): "Behold, for peace I had great bitterness," because the Holy One, blessed be He, answered him: "and I will defend this city, to save it, for My own sake, and for the sake of David My servant" (II Kings 19:34) — for as our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 10b): whoever attributes something to his own merit is made to depend on the merit of others.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:23: Behold, then, that a person should not even take credit for his own good deeds, and all the more so should not exalt and raise himself up because of them.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:24: And indeed, all this is what one should recall in his heart if he were like Abraham, like Moses, like Aaron, like David, and the other pious ones we have mentioned;
Mesillat Yesharim 22:25: but we, orphans of orphans, do not even need all this, for we already have so many deficiencies that no great reflection is needed to see our own lowliness, and how all our wisdom is counted as nothing.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:26: For the greatest sage among us is but a student of students compared to those of earlier generations. This is what we should truly understand and know, and let our hearts not be lifted up over nothing; rather, let us recognize that our understanding is light and our intellect exceedingly weak, that folly is great within us and error prevails, and that what we do know is but the very least of the least. If so, then, self-exaltation is certainly not fitting for us at all, but only shame and lowliness — and this is simple.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:27: Now, we have spoken up to here of humility of thought; let us now speak of humility of deed, which divides into four parts: conducting oneself with lowliness; bearing insults; hating mastery and fleeing from honor; and giving honor to all.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:28: The first is conducting oneself with lowliness, and this should be evident in his speech, his walking, his sitting, and all his movements.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:29: In his speech, they said, of blessed memory (Yoma 86a): a person's speech should always be gentle with people; and Scripture says explicitly (Ecclesiastes 9:17): "the words of the wise are heard in quiet." His words should be words of honor, not words of disgrace; and so it says (Proverbs 11:12): "He who is void of wisdom despises his neighbor." And it says (Proverbs 18:3): "when the wicked comes, contempt comes also."
Mesillat Yesharim 22:30: In his walking, they said, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 88b): they sent word from there: Who has a share in the World to Come? One who is humble and lowly of spirit, who bows down as he goes in and bows down as he goes out.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:31: He should not walk with an erect posture, nor with great heaviness, heel beside toe, but as everyone walks about their business; and so they said, of blessed memory (Kiddushin 31a): whoever walks with an erect posture is as though he pushes against the feet of the Divine Presence, and it is written (Isaiah 10:33): "and the haughty of stature shall be hewn down."
Mesillat Yesharim 22:32: In his sitting, that his place should be among the lowly, not among the high — and this too is stated explicitly in Scripture (Proverbs 25:6-7): "Do not glorify yourself before the king, and do not stand in the place of great men, etc." And so they said, of blessed memory (Vayikra Rabbah 1): distance yourself from your place two or three seats, and sit, until they say to you, "Go up" — and do not go up until they say to you, "Go down."
Mesillat Yesharim 22:33: And concerning everyone who makes himself small, they said, of blessed memory (Bava Metzia 85b): whoever makes himself small over words of Torah in this world becomes great in the World to Come.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:34: And correspondingly they said (Yalkut Shimoni, Ezekiel 361): "remove the turban and lift off the crown" (Ezekiel 21:31) — whoever is great in this world is small in the World to Come, and conversely, whoever is small in this world, his time of greatness will be in the World to Come.
Mesillat Yesharim 22:35: And they said (Sotah 5a): a person should always learn from the mind of his Maker, for the Holy One, blessed be He, left aside all the mountains and hills and rested His Presence upon Mount Sinai, and this is because of its lowliness.
